paragraphs: Consider, however, a board that responds to this distinction by asking reviewers to imagine that they do not know which structure failed. Such a procedure may reduce the tendency to treat what became obvious afterwards as if it had been obvious before. It cannot, merely by withholding the outcome, reproduce the information available to an inspector: reviewers may possess technical knowledge acquired only because the failure prompted research. What must be reconstructed is therefore not ignorance of the result alone, but the relation between the evidence then obtainable and the practical demands under which a decision had to be made.

This reconstruction creates a second danger. If the conditions of work are described so generously that every omission appears inevitable, contextual understanding becomes a vocabulary for exemption rather than an instrument of judgement. Conversely, to demand that an inspector should have investigated every conceivable defect would make the standard impossible to satisfy, thereby obscuring the difference between an unreasonable omission and an unavoidable limit. A board needs to ask which further inquiry was both feasible and warranted, not whether perfect foresight would have prevented the loss. The relevant alternative is an action that could reasonably have been taken, rather than an imaginary decision from which uncertainty has disappeared.

Suppose records show that both inspectors received a warning which could have been checked at modest cost, but that only the first structure encountered the storm. The common omission would then support criticism of both, although the damage might still matter for questions of repair and compensation. Had the warning been unavailable, the same pattern of damage would not by itself establish the same failure of care. Distinguishing these judgements does not make the outcome irrelevant; it prevents a fact whose significance varies with the question being asked from supplying an answer to every question. A fair review can consequently learn from a disaster without treating those whom chance spared as having demonstrated a competence they were never required to exercise. The distinction would also guide what future training should address: the missed inquiry, not merely the misfortune that exposed it.

The new procedure, however, could itself reproduce the closure it was introduced to remedy. Imagine that an applicant explains why caring for a relative requires a longer journey, only to be told that the explanation is admissible once converted into additional distance points. The testimony has entered the record, but the original assumption may remain untouched: need is still recognized only insofar as it can be represented by journey length. An opportunity to speak is not yet an opportunity to put the organizing principle of a decision in question.

That does not mean that a cooperative must abandon comparable scores whenever a narrative fails to fit them. Rooms remain limited, and decisions require reasons that others can inspect rather than exceptions whose force depends entirely on who presents them. What matters is whether the refusal to alter a category can itself be defended to those whose circumstances it excludes. A rule may survive such criticism; its survival after an answer has been given is different from its survival because no relevant objection was allowed to be heard.

Nor would accountability be secured simply by transferring discretion from programmers to a panel. A panel whose members accept unusual circumstances without explaining how they bear on allocation could make the process less predictable while leaving the grounds of authority equally inaccessible. The alternative to a closed calculation is not necessarily an unexplained personal judgement. It is a procedure in which the reasons for retaining, modifying or overriding a category are recorded in a form that later applicants can question, even when those reasons do not yield the result they wanted.

The cooperative might therefore publish examples of rejected as well as accepted challenges, identifying which assumptions were reconsidered and which constraints remained. Such a record would not eliminate disagreement, and it might disclose inconsistencies that a summary of successful appeals would conceal. Precisely for that reason, it could make correction possible. The institution would be accountable not because every applicant could obtain an exception, but because the boundary between a relevant circumstance and an irrelevant one would no longer be protected merely by the authority of whoever had drawn it.

A further test of this account would ask what could count against it. Suppose an earlier passage showed the daughter completing a difficult conversation without hesitation. The critic could not reasonably dismiss the scene merely because it interrupted a convenient pattern; nor would a single contrary episode automatically destroy every proposed connection. Its significance would depend on whether the interpretation could explain the difference without inventing a condition for which the novel supplied no evidence.

For example, the completed conversation might concern a stranger, whereas the abandoned ones concern the father. If that distinction were sustained elsewhere, what appeared to be a counterexample could specify the pattern more precisely. If it occurred nowhere else and served only to protect the reading from criticism, invoking it would risk turning explanation into an arrangement under which no detail could ever count as an objection.

The question is thus not how many details a critic can collect in favour of a conclusion already preferred. A reading gains strength when it makes connections that can be challenged by further attention to the work, rather than treating every possible feature as confirmation. To acknowledge this constraint is not to demand the sort of experiment through which a physical hypothesis might be tested; it is to distinguish responsiveness to a text from ingenuity unconstrained by it.

The first reviewer's dissatisfaction may consequently remain reasonable even if the second reading explains the formal pattern well. An account of how an ending works does not settle whether the experience it offers is satisfying, just as understanding why a character hesitates does not settle whether she ought to do so. These disagreements concern related but distinguishable judgements, none of which gains authority merely by borrowing the vocabulary of another.

An unresolved ending can therefore support more than one defensible response without making every response equally defensible. The critic's task is to show what a reading illuminates, what it leaves unexplained and which judgement is actually at issue. Where those distinctions disappear, either the author's presumed intention becomes an answer to questions it cannot settle, or the reader's freedom becomes a reason never to answer to the work at all.

A planner might reply that the form must eventually produce information from which a decision can be made, and that refusal to state a price leaves the authority unable to compare competing demands. There is force in this objection: recording disagreement is not the same as resolving a transport problem. Yet it does not follow that whatever cannot be entered as a price has already been shown to lack public relevance. A procedure which first excludes a reason and then cites its absence from the results as evidence of agreement has mistaken an effect of its own design for a discovery about the people consulted.

Consider a revised form that allows a resident to support transport improvements while rejecting the proposed removal, or to discuss compensation conditionally without accepting removal as justified. These positions can coexist without inconsistency because the questions concern different stages of a decision. Unless that conditional structure is preserved when responses are summarized, a willingness to negotiate after an adverse decision may be reported as prior consent to it. The authority would then appear to have consulted a wider range of positions while converting them back into the narrower language whose adequacy was disputed. Adding a space for comments is insufficient if the method of counting answers erases the distinctions the comments were meant to express.

This does not establish that the garden must prevail over an urgent need for transport, nor that decisions must wait until every kind of value has been translated into a common measure. An authority may have to decide between claims for which no agreed scale exists. Its obligation is then to explain why one consideration was given priority, rather than to claim that the consultation had dissolved the conflict. Compensation may remain appropriate after such a decision without retrospectively showing that the loss was acceptable to those compensated. What openness protects is not a right to secure the preferred outcome, but a difference between being overruled for stated reasons and having one's disagreement represented as a preference one never expressed.

The demand for independence needs a qualification of its own. Instruments operating on different principles may still share a calibration standard, a procedure for selecting observations or a mathematical assumption used to process them. To call the second comparison independent simply because the machines look different would repeat, at another level, the inference challenged in the first place. Independence must be specified with respect to a possible source of agreement, not awarded to a device as though it were an intrinsic property.

This does not require a search for a method dependent on nothing. Such a search would leave the researchers unable even to compare measurements, since comparison itself requires some shared conventions. The question is which shared elements could generate the particular pattern under investigation in the absence of the effect proposed to explain it.

Suppose the researchers vary the calibration while retaining the new instruments, and one disputed pattern disappears. That result would give them a reason to examine the calibration's role, but it would not prove that every measurement made with it had been mistaken. They would still need an account of why the dependence mattered to this inference rather than merely note that a dependence existed.

An alternative explanation can also be too accommodating. If it is adjusted after each comparison so that any conceivable result is said to follow from an unspecified flaw, it ceases to identify a vulnerability that inquiry can distinguish from the original explanation. Suspicion has then been preserved by making its object impossible to locate.

A useful criticism must therefore expose its own proposal to questions about what would strengthen or weaken it. This obligation does not make critics responsible for supplying a complete replacement theory before they may raise a difficulty; it requires them to distinguish a specific unresolved possibility from a general declaration that something could always be wrong.

Confidence earned through such comparisons remains conditional, but conditionality need not make it arbitrary. Its strength lies in knowing which alternatives have been examined and which dependencies remain consequential, rather than in an imagined escape from dependence. The disagreement contributes to knowledge when it changes what the agreement can reasonably be taken to establish.
